blocks.html: Although death is the end of all evils, the rest from all misery, and a strong bulwark against the calamities of this world —

notes.citation: A Latin hexameter on death — source not identified
notes.original: Illa malis requiem finemq́; laboribus affert.
notes.gloss: Perhaps a humanist line or Coras's own; it is not Virgil, Ovid, Horace or Seneca in this form.

blocks.html: It brings to our ills rest, and to our labours an end (Illa malis requiem finemque laboribus affert).

And although for that reason it ought not to be dreaded by a man of worth, but rather contemned and despised a2; and although Numantius, writing to Marcus Cicero, says that one ought often to desire an honest death, by which a man passes beyond innumerable perils and crosses of the inconstant fortune of this miserable world — so far is it from being a thing one ought to flee b; and although Saint Paul burned with a continual desire and ardent zeal to attain to the heavenly inheritance, and to be separated from the body, to dwell with Jesus Christ c: nevertheless, to wish at certain times, and for some vexation that befalls, for the last sigh and period of one's life, is the speech of a person too much subject to her passions, and, for the rest, ill instructed in the law of God; of whom, being his vassals and most bounden servants, we must wait upon all his commandments. And, as Hegesippus said, we must not wish to depart from this world sooner, nor to remain in it longer, than the good God who has given us being and life wills and commands it. And it is not lawful to cut the thread of life, or to dissolve the soul from the body, for any other than him who joined it. And just as Plato says that those who by authority of the magistrate are made prisoners must not go out of the prison before the magistrate by whose authority they were put in orders it, so neither must we, without the will of the Lord God who has given us the soul, drive it from us, draw it out, or put it forth from the prison of this mortal and miserable body c2. Saint Augustine in a certain place occupies and labours himself greatly to show the great fault committed by those who desire, and still worse those who execute, a voluntary death upon their own persons, singularly when they do it for fear of punishment or of infamy d. Which before him Aristotle had learnedly discoursed, saying that it is not the act of a constant and virtuous man, but rather of a timid and cowardly one, to slay oneself with one's own hands, and to make oneself the cruel minister of one's own death, in order to flee punishment, poverty, or some other discontent e. I know well that in time past Hannibal, Cato, Cassius, Brutus, Nero, Diocletian, Sardanapalus, Cleopatra, and several others, so as not to fall into the hands of their enemies, killed themselves, or had themselves killed by their servants. And others have done no less from an impatience of grief, wearied by the martyrdom of some sad and lamentable passion f: as the Emperor Hadrian, and Silius Italicus, an excellent poet, both overcome by incredible torments of sickness; as also Lucretia and Porcia, Roman women — the one too much grieved by the outrage received from King Tarquin, who had raped her; the other greatly troubled at hearing of the death of Brutus her husband. And that others too, weary of dealing in the traffic of this world, have executed the same, to unburden the spirit of this mortal load and to set it at rest, in the beatitude they hoped for — as the Gymnosophists and Brahmans in the Indies; as Cleombrotus, the Ambraciot Philosopher, who, after having read Plato's Phaedo on the immortality of the soul, written in the person of Socrates, to seek a surer rest threw himself headlong from a high wall into the sea, so as the sooner to gain the company of the eternally happy g; of whom Ovid, speaking, said h:

notes.citation: Cicero, Letters to his Friends (Epistulae ad familiares), books V and VI — the consolatory letters of 46–45 BC (to Titius, Fam. 5.16; to Torquatus, 6.3–4; to Toranius, 6.21), where death is said to be no evil and even to be wished for in such times
notes.original: Ciceron au v. & vj. liure de ſes epiſt.

notes.citation: Cicero, Letters to his Friends 11.28.2, the letter of C. Matius to Cicero: numquam enim honestam mortem fugiendam, saepe etiam oppetendam putavi; Coras's "Numantius" is a slip or a wrong sort for Matius
notes.original: Ciceron au liure xi. deſd. epiſtres.

notes.citation: Philippians 1 (1:23: "having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ")

notes.gloss: Socrates: a man must not take his own life until God sends some necessity, as now to me; we are in a kind of guard-post (φρουρά), and the gods are our keepers. Coras turns the image into the prisoner who may not leave the magistrate's prison unbidden. The note is printed with the key c, repeating the key of the previous note; the transcription gives it c2.

notes.citation: Augustine, The City of God, book I, chapters 17 to 28 (1.17–27 treat suicide: the Christian women who killed themselves to escape rape, Lucretia, Cato, and the rule that no one may kill himself to avoid another's sin or his own shame)
notes.original: S-Auguſtin au i. liure de ciuita. Dei c. xvij. inſque au xxviij.
notes.gloss: The Loys Viues of the case file §7 is the commentator on this book; Coras here cites Augustine himself.

notes.citation: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, book IV chapter 7 as printed; the passage is III.7 (1116a12–15): to die to escape poverty or love or anything painful is the mark not of a brave man but of a coward (cf. V.11, 1138a, on the suicide's injustice to the city)
notes.original: Ariſtote au iiij. des Ethiques c. vij.

notes.citation: Digest 48.21.3 (De bonis eorum qui ante sententiam vel mortem sibi consciverunt vel accusatorem corruperunt, l. 3, Marcian)
notes.original: l. iii. D. de bon. eo. qui mort. ſibi cõſ.
notes.gloss: Those who kill themselves taedio vitae vel impatientia doloris aut iactationis — "from weariness of life or impatience of pain or from vainglory" — keep their testament and their goods pass to their heirs, as against those who die to escape a pending charge; Coras's impatience de douleur is the law's phrase.

notes.citation: Cicero, Tusculan Disputations I (1.84: Callimachus's epigram on Cleombrotus of Ambracia, who, nothing ill having befallen him, threw himself from a wall into the sea after reading Plato's book); and Lactantius, Divine Institutes III (De falsa sapientia philosophorum), chapter 18
notes.original: Ciceron au liure j. des Tu ſculanes. Lactance au iij. de falſæ ſa-pientia.
notes.gloss: Lactantius 3.18 reviews the suicides of the philosophers — Cleombrotus, Cato, Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus, Empedocles, Democritus — as the fruit of a false wisdom.
Vel de praecipiti venias in Tartara saxo, / ut qui Socraticum de nece legit opus — the print's tartara and its commas are kept in the French.

notes.citation: Callimachus, epigram 23 (Pfeiffer) = Palatine Anthology 7.471, in an anonymous Latin version — translator not identified
notes.original: Vita vale, muro præceps delapſus ab alto, Dixiſti moriens, Ambraciota puer. Nullum in morte malum, docti, ſed ſcripta Platonis, Non ita erant animo percipienda tuo.
notes.gloss: The Greek: Εἴπας "Ἥλιε χαῖρε" Κλεόμβροτος Ὡμβρακιώτης / ἥλατ' ἀφ' ὑψηλοῦ τείχεος εἰς Ἀΐδην, / ἄξιον οὐδὲν ἰδὼν θανάτου κακόν, ἀλλὰ Πλάτωνος / ἓν τὸ περὶ ψυχῆς γράμμ' ἀναλεξάμενος — "Saying 'Sun, farewell', Cleombrotus of Ambracia leapt from a high wall into Hades, having seen no evil worth dying for, but having read one writing of Plato, that on the soul." The Latin's docti is taken with Platonis, "of learned Plato"; its Nullum in morte malum has no verb and is translated as the maxim it states.

blocks.html: Or may you come into Tartarus from a steep rock, like him who read the Socratic work on death.
And Callimachus, a Greek poet, made upon him an elegant epigram, since rendered into Latin by some learned man, as follows:
"Life, farewell," you said as you died, Ambraciot youth, fallen headlong from the high wall. There is no evil in death; but the writings of learned Plato were not thus to be taken by your mind.

Others, for an ostentation and vain hope of eternising their memory, and to build themselves some trophy of honour in the ages to come, as Cleanthes, Chrysippus and Zeno in Greece <sup class="mk" data-key="i" data-page="p104">i</sup>; the Decii and the Curtii at Rome, Menoeceus at Thebes, Codrus King in Athens.

notes.citation: Lactantius, Divine Institutes III (De falsa sapientia), chapter 18
notes.original: Lactance au iij. de falſa ſapieria. c. xviij.
notes.gloss: The print's ſapieria (or ſapietia) is a wrong sort for sapientia; the same chapter as at {g}. Zeno, Cleanthes and Chrysippus, the Stoic masters, who are there said to have died by their own act.

blocks.html: Codrus, not afraid to die for his country (Codrus pro patria non timidus mori) k.

notes.gloss: Codrus pro patria non timidus mori: Codrus, the last king of Athens, who sought death in battle because the oracle had promised victory to the side whose king fell.

blocks.html: And several others, among whom Empedocles, that great Philosopher, who, to get himself esteemed a God, being near Mount Etna in Sicily, which ever burns, stole away from his companions and secretly threw himself into the fire, with the intention that, not appearing afterwards, he should be put among the number of the immortal gods; of whom Horace l: I shall tell it, and I shall recount the death of the Sicilian poet: Empedocles, while he longs to be held an immortal God, coldly leapt into burning Etna. Let it be right, and let poets be allowed to perish.

notes.gloss: Siculique poetae / narrabo interitum. deus immortalis haberi / dum cupit Empedocles, ardentem frigidus Aetnam / insiluit. sit ius liceatque perire poetis. The print's Dicam at the head of the quotation is not in Horace's text (whose line 462 ends nec sit mihi credere tantum) and is translated as Coras gives it, as part of the quotation; its immortalus is a wrong sort for immortalis, and Inſiluit ius, liceátque runs together insiluit. sit ius liceatque. The fifth-foot frigidus, "coldly", is Horace's joke, kept.

blocks.html: Nevertheless he was well frustrated of his hope: for the violence of the fire cast out the little slippers of tin which he used to wear, which uncovered all his ambition and imposture. Now, to come back to our sheep [reuenans à nos moutons: to our subject]: it is a very vile thing, cowardly, unworthy of a Christian, and most displeasing to God, to wish to forestall one's days, to slaughter and undo oneself with one's own hands before the Lord calls us; from whom we have in keeping the soul he has given us. And if you have taken into your keeping money, or rings, or other things of your friend, and misuse them, you are with very good reason esteemed wicked, disloyal and perverse: with greater cause, therefore, if you abuse, cast out and drive from you so precious a thing as is the soul, which God has committed to you and delivered into your keeping.
